answer.exemplar: The failure is what synchronises the population, and that is the whole point. One event knocks over every client at the same instant, so all two thousand begin counting the same thirty seconds together, and a service that has just restarted is handed two thousand requests in a single moment — the moment it has the least spare capacity it will have all day. The thirty seconds is not wrong because it is long or short; it is wrong because it is the same for everybody, and a constant is the one value that guarantees the retries collide with each other and with whatever else is recovering at that moment. Making the wait grow with each failure does two separate things: it keeps a client from hammering a service that is still down, and, once a random offset is added on top, it spreads the two thousand arrivals across the interval so that each second sees a fraction of the total instead of all of it. The number of attempts is not changed by any of this. What changes is their timing, and timing is what decides whether a recovery becomes a second outage.

questions.explanation: A fixed interval is a constant across a population, and a population that failed together starts counting together, so the constant guarantees that the retries land together. Making the wait grow with each failure keeps a client off a service that is still down; adding a random offset to that wait is what spreads a large population's arrivals across the interval, so the peak falls without the total changing. The damage is worst exactly where it is least welcome, since the retries arrive at the instant the service has just recovered and has the least spare capacity it will have that day.

answer.exemplar: The window exists to change a ratio, and the ratio is the reason it was introduced. One write for five hundred orders instead of one write per order means the table has to be sized for an average arrival rate rather than an instantaneous one, and the batch size gives a bound on how much work any single write must do — both worth having when the service is doing nothing but small writes. The charge is time, and it is the same fact seen from the other side: an order accepted at the top of a window waits nearly fifteen minutes to be in the table, and the mean wait is half the window, so efficiency has been bought with a promise the buyer has to be willing to keep. Nothing here removes that charge, because it is not a separate cost but the same fact as the batching. What a design change can shift is who absorbs it. Acknowledging on acceptance from a local durable write, and treating the batch as a separate later step, moves the wait off the caller's confirmation without touching the ratio that justified the window in the first place — the data still arrives on the same schedule, but the caller is no longer waiting for it.

questions.explanation: A window trades a ratio of writes against a delay, and the two are the same fact seen from opposite sides: fewer writes is exactly what produces a longer wait for any single order, with the worst case the full window and the mean half of it. The charge cannot be removed without giving up the batching, but it can be moved. Acknowledging on acceptance from a local durable write and letting the batch be a separate later step leaves the ratio untouched and takes the wait off the caller's confirmation, which is usually the promise the caller actually needs.
questions.hint: Ask what the fifteen minutes cost, and which of the two figures that cost is identical to.

questions.explanation: The order is forced by what a crash between any two steps would cost. Verification comes first because it is the only step that makes the rest safe: an unsigned or stale request should cost nothing, and the receiver is the only party that can compute the signature. The applied-set lookup comes next, because it is the only thing that stops the effect happening twice, and it has to precede the effect rather than follow it. answer.exemplar: A period is a claim about how long the job takes, and a claim is only as good as its worst observation. The seventy minutes here is what the job took on the day it was measured; the run that follows a slow dependency, the one that meets a much larger table, or the one that begins while the previous report is still being generated all take longer, and on that day the sixty-minute period is simply wrong. Lengthening the period moves the boundary without moving it correctly, so what it really buys is margin — a legitimate thing to buy when the job is a report nobody reads urgently and a missed run costs a day rather than an hour. A lock is a different kind of object. It predicts nothing and observes: a run that arrives while another is going declines to start, whatever the runtimes turn out to be. The two are not rivals, and the useful combination is a lock with a lease as the guarantee plus a period chosen with enough margin that the lock rarely has to refuse, because a design refusing ten runs a day has traded a race for an outage.

questions.explanation: A period asserts something about the job's duration that only its worst run can refute, and the run that meets a slow dependency or a larger table is exactly the one that was not measured. Lengthening the period therefore buys margin rather than correctness. A lock is a different kind of object: it predicts nothing and observes the present, so a run that arrives while another is going declines regardless of how long either takes. The two combine well, because a period with enough margin keeps the lock from refusing most starts.

answer.exemplar: The two mechanisms differ in where they keep the record of a change, and each fails in the place its own design cannot see. Polling reads a log the far side keeps, so anything that falls off the end of that log between two reads is gone: read hourly against a log holding a hundred entries and a busy provider, and the reader pages past changes it will never be offered again. The failure is invisible because both numbers look healthy — the log is being written, the reader is succeeding — and it becomes visible only if the provider also reports how far back its log reaches and the reader reports how far forward it has got, so the two numbers can be compared for a gap. A callback moves the record to the subscriber, and its characteristic failure is the request that never arrived: the endpoint was down, the address was wrong, the response was refused, and the change now exists only inside the sender's retry budget, which is finite. That failure is visible only if the subscriber publishes the newest identifier it has applied and the sender counts its delivery failures rather than logging them, because an absent callback is otherwise indistinguishable from a quiet day.

questions.explanation: Polling's gap is the interval, so a change made after one read and before the next is only found if the query asks for current state, and a change log read less often than it is written will page past entries. A callback's gap is the delivery attempt, so a change is lost when the subscriber is unreachable and the sender's finite retry budget decides how much of that is repaired. Both failures are invisible while the mechanism's own counters go unwatched, which is why a provider reporting how far back its log reaches and a subscriber reporting its newest applied identifier are the figures that make either visible.
questions.hint: Ask where each mechanism keeps the change, and what it therefore cannot see.
